newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. data enliven German shares in late trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. data enliven German shares in late trade.

text.p: German shares ended the day sharply ahead on Tuesday after softer-than-expected U.S. data fuelled a mini-rally on the bond market and a fresh burst of interest in financial shares.

Giant insurer Allianz AG, in demand because of its large fixed-income securities portfolio, led the late advance which took the IBIS DAX index up 1.6 percent or 52.90 points to end late electronic dealings at 3,425.86 points.
The DAX had closed the bourse session at mid-afternoon some 40 points lower, but still up 20.13 points at 3.383.19 points.
The U.S. data, comprising employment costs, durable goods orders and a business confidence report, were released in early afternoon, European time.
Market heavyweight Allianz ended up 4.39 percent at 335.10 marks, spurting ahead with other financials in late trade.
Deutsche Bank rose 2.10 marks to 90.47 marks amid heavy trading, while Bayerische Vereinsbank rose 1.58 marks, or 2.36 percent, to 68.40 marks.
Reinsurer Munich Re ended the day up 95 marks, or 2.3 percent at 4,155 marks.
"The sheer scale of these holdings, especially in fixed income, are being reflected here," said BHF Bank AG banking and insurance analyst Dieter Hein.
Engineering giant Siemens AG also outperformed to end the day up 2.9 percent at 93.05 marks. Dealers cited a variety of technical buy signals as the reason for its popularity.
At the other end of the scale, chemicals firm Degussa slid to end the day down 2.6 percent at 77.95 marks after releasing first-half earnings.

The company reported a 25 percent gain in first half profits and gave an optimistic outlook for the second half but its sales figure of 7.2 billion marks was at the lower end of expectations, dealers said.
"Selling on good news" was another factor, traders said.

With Wall Street looking strong in early dealings, the IBIS DAX was seen defending the 3,400 point level, a key resistance point, but prices may wane before the Thursday May Day holiday, dealers warned.
"Things are certainly positive in the very short term but I wouldn't see this as real euphoria," said a Stuttgart dealer.
